prompt: Discuss Aristotle's account of phantasia and its role in practical reasoning, drawing on De Anima III.3 and the relevant commentators.

## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis

Aristotle's account of φαντασία in *De Anima* III.3 occupies a decisive juncture between his treatment of αἴσθησις and his investigation of νοῦς, such that the image-making faculty cannot be understood apart from the prior operation of sense-perception, yet neither can it be collapsed into perception itself. (Aristotle 2014, *Rhetoric*, p. sight or seeing: imagination takes place in the absence of both, as e.g. in dreams" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). This passage establishes the fundamental contrast between φαντασία and αἴσθησις: whereas perception requires the actual presence of an external sensible object to actualize the faculty, phantasia operates in conditions where no such object is present, thus demonstrating a functional independence that separates it from the perceptual act even though it remains causally dependent upon prior perceptual episodes. White reports that Aristotle's treatment of phantasia in *De Anima* III.3 occurs at a critical juncture between his account of sensation and his account of νοῦς, thereby positioning the faculty as an indispensable intermediary in the soul's progression from sensory receptivity to intellectual cognition (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). Papachristou further confirms that *De Anima* III.3 is the primary locus of Aristotle's discussion of phantasia, and her analysis of phantasia's kinds is grounded in a reading of the relevant chapters and passages of that treatise (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 6–7). Accordingly, Aristotle's graded distinction between sensitive phantasia and deliberative phantasia — to which we shall return in subsequent sections — already presupposes this initial differentiation from aisthesis, insofar as even the lowest grade of phantasia involves a residual movement persisting after sensation has ceased, whereas perception demands the concurrent operation of sense-organ and sensible object. The relation to δόξα and the question of voluntariness will be addressed explicitly in Section 4 below. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia

The φάντασμα, as the product of φαντασία, constitutes the quasi-perceptual content that persists after the sensory encounter has ended and that furnishes the material upon which both memory and intellection subsequently operate. Aristotle insists that the soul never thinks without a phantasma, thereby establishing the phantasma as an indispensable mediating term between sensory experience and noetic activity; indeed, phantasmata serve as the representational content through which practical and theoretical reasoning alike proceed (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). Caston's analysis illuminates the distinctive intentional structure of the phantasma by drawing attention to its capacity for falsity: Aristotle "says that a scene-painting or a dream are both 'something, but not what they produce a phantasia of'" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). This observation is crucial, for it reveals that the phantasma possesses a representational content that can diverge from the way things actually are — it presents something as something, yet what it presents need not correspond to any actual state of affairs. Hence the phantasma introduces a species of intentionality distinct from veridical perception, one which makes error structurally possible. The graded character of phantasia bears directly upon the nature of the phantasma: at the level of sensitive phantasia, the phantasma retains close fidelity to the original sensory impression, whereas at the level of deliberative phantasia, phantasmata are combined, compared, and manipulated in the service of practical reasoning, producing composite images that guide action toward future ends. 10–12). The voluntariness of phantasmatic production — particularly salient in deliberative contexts — and its relation to belief will be treated more fully below. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme

The relationship between φαντασία and μνήμη discloses a further dimension of phantasia's functional architecture, for memory depends upon the phantasma as its essential medium while nevertheless remaining distinct from the image-making faculty itself. (Aristotle 2014, *Rhetoric*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), "All memory, therefore, implies a time elapsed; consequently only those animals which perceive time remember, and the organ whereby they perceive time is also that whereby they remember" (Aristotle, *On Memory*, p. 1). Memory thus presupposes not merely the retention of a phantasma but the capacity to apprehend temporal distance — to register that the phantasma belongs to a past perceptual episode rather than to a present sensation. This temporal indexing differentiates mneme from phantasia proper; the phantasma in memory functions with a dual aspect, simultaneously presenting its content and indicating that this content was previously perceived. Caston recognizes that Aristotle's account of phantasia demands precisely such an intentional structure, one that "makes error possible" and whose "content" must "be explained in a different way" than that of straightforward perception (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, p. 18). Thus while phantasia supplies the representational material for memory, it is memory's distinctive temporal reference that converts the phantasma from a free-floating image into a genuine recollection. The distinction between sensitive and deliberative grades of phantasia is operative here as well: animals possessing only sensitive phantasia may retain phantasmata and exhibit rudimentary memory, yet deliberative phantasia — requiring λόγος — enables the complex temporal synthesis characteristic of human recollection and practical deliberation (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 20–22). The question of phantasia's relation to doxa, and the specific voluntariness that characterizes deliberative image-making, is addressed in the section that follows. 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa

The differentiation of φαντασία from δόξα constitutes one of the most consequential argumentative achievements of *De Anima* III.3, for it secures phantasia's status as a sui generis psychological capacity irreducible to belief or judgment. Aristotle's strategy proceeds by noting that phantasia can be false without entailing conviction, whereas doxa necessarily involves commitment to a truth-claim and thus implicates πίστις; accordingly, some non-rational animals possess imagination without possessing rational discourse, thereby demonstrating that phantasia does not presuppose the λόγος upon which belief depends (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). This structural point is reinforced by Aristotle's broader account of animal movement, where "thinking and imagination, as we said above, produce that which brings about the affections, since they produce the forms which bring them about" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). Here phantasia operates as a proximate cause of desire and locomotion independently of any doxastic assent, confirming its explanatory priority in the practical domain. White's careful exegesis underscores that Aristotle's De Anima contains only sparse references to phantasia before III.3, suggesting that the dedicated treatment was designed precisely to establish these distinctions with systematic rigor (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotle's anthropology further illuminates the practical stakes: the human being is defined as living "a life, specifically one that is πρακτική, of such a being as has language" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 46). Within this practical life, deliberative phantasia — dependent upon φρόνησις and rational discourse — enables the agent to compose and evaluate alternative courses of action through the voluntary manipulation of phantasmata; sensitive phantasia, by contrast, operates involuntarily in response to residual perceptual movements. Thus phantasia explains doxa not by reducing to it but by providing the representational substratum upon which belief, judgment, and ultimately practical reasoning are built.
